name: Exosome hair therapy
lead: Exosome hair therapy refers to scalp treatments, applied as serums, through microneedling or by injection, that contain exosomes: nanometre-scale vesicles released by cells that carry proteins, lipids and nucleic acids. Clinics and cosmetic brands that offer it say the vesicles, usually derived from cultured mesenchymal stem cells such as umbilical cord cells, signal to dormant follicles and prompt regrowth. [10]

Exosomes are a real and active subject of biomedical research, but their use in hair loss is at an early stage. Registered trials exist for androgenetic alopecia and self-perceived thinning, mostly small (about 15 to 100 participants) and many labelled early phase or not applicable. [1][2][3][5][9] No peer-reviewed efficacy results from these trials have been published, so the effectiveness of the approach has not been established.
In the United States, the FDA has stated that exosome products are drug products that require premarket approval, and Wikipedia notes advisories about noncompliant marketing. [10]

The appearance case that practitioners make is thicker, denser-looking hair. A 2024 prospective study in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery followed 30 men with androgenetic alopecia after a single scalp session of exosomes derived from foreskin mesenchymal stromal cells and reported a rise in mean hair density from about 150 to 157 hairs per square centimetre over 12 weeks.[12] Reviewers of the wider literature describe the field as early, with small studies and few controlled designs.[12]

paras: Exosomes are membrane-bound extracellular vesicles roughly 30 to 150 nm across, formed inside cells and released when internal compartments fuse with the cell surface. They are proposed to carry cargo that mediates cell-to-cell communication, although Wikipedia notes that evidence for functional RNA transfer in mammals remains limited. [10]

In hair treatments, preparations are typically described as 'exosome serums' or 'regenerative complexes' applied to the scalp, sometimes alongside microneedling. Registered trials name products such as a BENEV exosome complex, an exosome product delivered by microneedling, and umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cell exosomes. [3][8][7]

Exosomes were first observed in maturing reticulocytes in 1983, and the name was applied by Johnstone's group in 1987; their later recognition as carriers of RNA and protein is what drove interest in using them as signals between cells.[10] Wikipedia's account of the field lists early or preclinical work on wound healing, joint pain, cardiac repair and autoimmune conditions, and notes that some clinics market exosome skincare with claims such as wrinkle reduction.[10]

Hair is one of several cosmetic targets. Marketing for exosome hair treatments typically draws on the idea that vesicles from stem cells can influence the follicle's growth cycle, a mechanism that researchers are still investigating rather than one with an established clinical record.[10][12]

Hair-loss trials involving exosomes are registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, and no peer-reviewed results for them are cited in this article. Registered studies include a completed 24-person trial of exosome treatment and hair growth (NCT06930326) [1], a completed 30-person phase 3 study in androgenetic alopecia (NCT06539273) [2], a 30-person study of a BENEV exosome complex for self-perceived thinning [3], and a 100-person phase 1 study of 'Age Zero' exosomes in men and women with androgenetic alopecia whose status is listed as unknown [5].

Other registrations include an early phase 1 study that was terminated (n=16) [4], a combined device and exosome study in hair thinning [6], a recruiting phase 1/2 study of umbilical cord stem cell exosomes in young men with androgenetic alopecia (n=59) [7], a pilot of microneedle-delivered exosomes in women (n=15) [8], and a 50-person study of umbilical cord stem cell exosomes [9]. A registration alone does not mean a study has been reviewed or approved, and does not report its outcomes. [11]

The 2024 Aesthetic Plastic Surgery study was a single-arm trial, with no control or saline group, of 30 men aged 22 to 65 with Norwood-Hamilton type III to VI hair loss who did not use hair-loss medications. Participants received one session of foreskin-derived mesenchymal stromal cell exosomes into the scalp and were assessed at 4 and 12 weeks with Trichoscan dermatoscopic counts. Mean density went from 149.7 hairs per square centimetre at baseline to 153.6 at week 4 and 157.0 at week 12, and patient-reported scores also changed. No adverse events were reported during follow-up.[12] The authors listed the lack of a control group, the short follow-up and the absence of repeat treatment among the study's limits.[12]

Wikipedia reports that the FDA considers exosome products to be drugs requiring premarket approval, and that it issued an advisory in late 2019 about noncompliant marketing following patient injuries in Nebraska, with further cautions to firms in 2020. [10] Those events concerned exosome products generally rather than hair treatments specifically. Safety data from the hair-specific trials cited here are not available.

The FDA's December 2019 public safety notification states that there are currently no FDA-approved exosome products, that exosomes used to treat disease are generally regulated as drugs and biological products requiring premarket review, and that the agency had received reports of serious adverse events in Nebraska patients treated with unapproved exosome products.[13] The FDA asks health professionals and consumers to report problems through MedWatch, and advises people considering an exosome treatment to ask whether the FDA has reviewed it and to request its Investigational New Drug number.[13]

card.summary: Scalp serums or injections of cell-derived vesicles sold as follicle revivers; only small registered trials so far.
card.note: FDA describes exosome products as unapproved drugs; no peer-reviewed hair outcomes cited.

quick.overview:
Exosome hair therapy applies vesicles released by cultured cells, often umbilical cord stem cells, to the scalp as a serum, via microneedling, or by injection. Providers say the vesicles signal to follicles and support regrowth.

Small trials are registered for androgenetic alopecia and thinning hair, but this article cites registrations rather than published results, so efficacy is not established.
quick.mechanism: Exosomes are proposed to carry proteins and nucleic acids that mediate cell-to-cell signalling; Wikipedia notes functional RNA transfer in mammals is not firmly shown. Hair-specific mechanisms are claimed by providers rather than demonstrated in cited work.
quick.risks: The FDA has said exosome products are drugs requiring premarket approval and has reported advisories about noncompliant marketing and injuries in Nebraska (not hair-specific). Hair-specific safety data are not available in the cited sources.
